subject: Number of detections increases further from 0

messages.author: 2da0cb5a6c1a8641
messages.subject: Number of detections increases further from 0
parts:
I created distance intervals and placed observations in bins during the survey (we were not permitted to get exact distances in the field). I have a centerline and 3 bins of increasing width. I made a distance histogram for each of my ten surveys and almost all of them have the fewest detections in the 0 bin and the number of detections increases the further you get away from the centerline (see attached pdf). I have looked at other topics in the forum and in the Intro DS book and have noticed that evasive movements can cause fewer detections closer to the centerline. However, I believe the issue is that the animals were not uniformly distributed and the survey lines were not randomly placed with respect to that distribution.


I know that binning in the field is not recommended and 5-7 bins is much better than only 4. Also, I know that lines should be randomly placed with respect to animal distribution. However, I am wondering what issues might arise with fitting a detection function or deriving a density estimate from a dataset with these issues. 


Thanks,


Bradley

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Number of detections increases further from 0
parts:
Bradley:

We'll need a bit more information to provide advice.  Specifically, we will need information on the width of your bins.  Technically speaking your centreline is of width zero.  What are the cutpoints used in the histograms you provided?

You are right in all of the issues you raised: evasive movement, non-random transect placement, exact distances in the field, large numbers of bins.  If it is truly the case that number of detections (per unit area) actually increase at increasing distances from the transect, then a decreasing detection function cannot be fitted to such data and no useful estimate of density can be determined.  If your study organism knows where your transects are located (and either loves or hates those locations) then the number of detections at various distances from the transect is not solely caused by the detection function, but is a product of both the detection process (observation model) and distribution of animals (state model).

parts:
In Reply to My Early Post:

Our distance surveys on alligators were conducted at night using spotlights. Each night's survey route was considered a transect and was replicated 5 times in the same season. We had two routes total and they both went through two different habitats (narrow river or stream and large open bay or reservoir). I assume the two habitat types in each transect (route) are considered strata, but they could be broken up into two separate surveys (I think).

Intervals on each side of the transect are >0 to 25 m, 25 to 50 m, and 50 m to the shore which varies along the transect (mean is around 75 m). Also, the centerline only included individuals at 0.

Unfortunately, I think the conplications of working in our study system and my lack of understanding of field methods in DS before surveying has precluded a proper analysis. But i would love your feedback.

I truly appreciate any help. If you would like to provide any off list serv advice my email is bas273(at)msstate.edu

Bradley

messages.author: 2da0cb5a6c1a8641
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Number of detections increases further from 0
parts:
Thanks for all of the help and advice. After further discussion with Dr. Rexstad, I believe that my data is not fit for distance sampling because of the reasons listed in my previous posts. But most importantly, we conducted our boat-based surveys in the center of the channel (non-random placement of transect) even when alligators were not uniformly distributed at all distances from the boat.

-Bradley
